sin.title: Why sin θ = y
steps: P is where the angle's side crosses the circle. Dropping a vertical line from P to the x-axis forms a right triangle (one of its angles is 90°).
The hypotenuse is the longest side, the one opposite the right angle. Here it's the circle's radius, which is 1.
Definition of sine. The opposite side is the one facing θ, not touching it: the point's height.
Substitute: the opposite side is y and the hypotenuse is 1.
Dividing by 1 changes nothing.
sin.use: You can read the sine straight off the drawing: it's the height (y-coordinate) of P.

cos.title: Why cos θ = x
steps: As with sine, P and its shadow on the x-axis form a right triangle.
The hypotenuse is the circle's radius.
Definition of cosine. The adjacent side is the one touching θ (other than the hypotenuse): the triangle's base.
The base is x and the hypotenuse is 1.
cos.use: Cosine is P's x-coordinate: how far the point has moved horizontally.

tan.title: Why the yellow segment is tan θ
steps: Definition of tangent in a right triangle. In the small triangle the opposite side is y and the adjacent side is x.
Extend the angle's side to the line x = 1: a big triangle appears with base 1 and height t (the yellow segment). The symbol ∼ means "similar".
Both triangles have the same angles (they share θ and both have 90°). They are similar: same shape, different size, so their sides are proportional.
Solve for t. The yellow segment is exactly the tangent. It's named that because the line x = 1 touches the circle at a single point: it's tangent.
tan.use: Tangent is the slope of the angle's line: how much it rises per unit it moves forward.

cot.title: Why the blue segment is cot θ
steps: Definition: cotangent is the reciprocal of tangent.
Extend the angle's side to the horizontal line y = 1. This forms a triangle with height 1 and base c (the blue segment).
The line y = 1 is parallel to the x-axis, and the diagonal crosses both at the same angle (alternate angles).
From that corner, the opposite side is 1 and the adjacent side is c: tangent = opposite / adjacent.
Solve for c.
cot.use: It's the reciprocal of the slope; it shows up when studying nearly vertical lines.

sec.title: Why the red segment is sec θ
steps: It's the same big triangle as for tangent: base 1, height t. Its hypotenuse h is the red segment, from the origin to the line x = 1.
Definition of cosine applied to the big triangle: the adjacent side is 1 and the hypotenuse is h.
Solve for h. That's why |sec θ| is always 1 or more: the hypotenuse is never shorter than the base.
sec.use: It appears in physics (components of inclined forces) and in integrals.

csc.title: Why the green segment is csc θ
steps: It's the cotangent triangle: base c, height 1. Its hypotenuse h is the green segment, from the origin to the line y = 1.
The angle θ sits at the corner (c, 1). From there, the opposite side is 1.
Solve for h.
csc.use: Completes the six ratios; useful for simplifying expressions with 1/sin.

rad.title: Degrees and radians
steps: Length L of a circle of radius r.
On the unit circle a full turn has length 2π.
A radian is the angle spanning an arc (⌒) equal to the radius. That's why a full turn has 2π radians.
The same turn measured two ways. Divide by 2.
Rule of three: multiply by π/180 to get radians; by 180/π to go back to degrees.
rad.use: Physics and calculus formulas (e.g. the derivatives of sin and cos) only work in radians.

signs.title: Signs by quadrant
steps: Sine has the sign of y and cosine the sign of x.
Top right: all positive.
Top left: only sine (and its reciprocal, cosecant) is positive.
Bottom left: sin and cos are negative, but tan = y/x is negative/negative = positive.
Bottom right: only cosine (and secant) is positive.
A ratio and its reciprocal always share their sign (∼), because 1 divided by a number keeps its sign.
signs.use: Work out any angle with its reference angle: table value + quadrant sign.

notables.title: Where the key angles come from
steps: If one acute angle is 45°, so is the other (they add up to 90°). Both legs are equal; call them a. Apply Pythagoras with hypotenuse 1.
Solve for a. Rationalising means multiplying top and bottom by √2 to remove the root from the denominator.
Both legs have the same length.
An equilateral triangle (three equal sides) has three 60° angles. Cut in half, it gives two 30°-60°-90° triangles with hypotenuse 1.
The base b is split into two halves. The height h comes from Pythagoras: h² = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4.
Opposite 30° is the short base; opposite 60° is the height.
notables.use: With two triangles you can rebuild the whole table without memorising it.

rec-sin.title: sin θ · csc θ = 1
steps: Definition of cosecant: the reciprocal of sine.
Substitute the cosecant.
A number divided by itself is 1. Only valid if sin θ ≠ 0 (you can't divide by 0).
rec-sin.use: That's why they're called reciprocal ratios: multiplied together they give 1. It lets you switch from one to the other.

rec-cos.title: cos θ · sec θ = 1
steps: Definition of secant: the reciprocal of cosine.
Substitute the secant.
It simplifies, as long as cos θ ≠ 0.
rec-cos.use: If you know the cosine, the secant is its reciprocal (and vice versa).

rec-tan.title: tan θ · cot θ = 1
steps: Write both in terms of sine and cosine.
Multiply.
To multiply fractions, multiply top by top and bottom by bottom. Top and bottom are the same: 1.
rec-tan.use: Switch from tangent to cotangent with cot θ = 1/tan θ.

quot-tan.title: tan θ = sin θ / cos θ
steps: Definition of tangent in the right triangle.
On the unit circle the opposite side is y and the adjacent side is x.
Because y = sin θ and x = cos θ.
quot-tan.use: It's how you find the tangent when you only know sine and cosine.

quot-cot.title: cot θ = cos θ / sin θ
steps: Definition of cotangent: the tangent flipped over.
On the unit circle.
Replace x and y with cosine and sine.
quot-cot.use: Writing everything in sine and cosine is the first step to simplifying almost any expression.

pyth.title: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
steps: Pythagoras' theorem: in a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse (c) is the sum of the squares of the legs (a and b).
On the unit circle the legs are x and y, and the hypotenuse is the radius.
Substitute.
Replace x with cos θ and y with sin θ.
We write cos²θ instead of (cos θ)²; it's just notation.
The order of addition doesn't matter.
pyth.use: If you know one ratio you get the other: cos θ = ±√(1 − sin²θ). It's the basis of almost every other identity.

pyth-tan.title: 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ
steps: Start from the Pythagorean identity.
Divide every term by cos²θ (allowed if cos θ ≠ 0). Doing the same to both sides keeps the equality.
sin/cos is tan, cos/cos is 1 and 1/cos is sec.
Reorder. In the figure it's Pythagoras in the big triangle: legs 1 and tan θ, hypotenuse sec θ.
pyth-tan.use: Go from tangent to secant without finding the angle; it shows up a lot in integrals.

pyth-cot.title: 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ
steps: Start from the Pythagorean identity.
Now divide by sin²θ (if sin θ ≠ 0).
sin/sin is 1, cos/sin is cot and 1/sin is csc. It's Pythagoras in the triangle on the line y = 1.
pyth-cot.use: Links cotangent and cosecant just as the previous one links tangent and secant.

sum-cos.title: Cosine of a sum and a difference
steps: Two points on the unit circle, at angles α and β. The angle between them is α − β. We'll compute the distance d between A and B in two ways.
Distance formula between two points: (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)².
Expand each square with (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b².
Group the squares of each angle.
Each coloured bracket equals 1 because sin² + cos² = 1.
Second way: rotate the figure until B lies on the x-axis. Rotating doesn't change distances, so A′B′ is also d.
Same distance formula. Expanding, sin² + cos² gives 1 again.
Both expressions are the same distance, so they're equal.
Subtract 2 from both sides and divide by −2. That's the difference formula.
For the sum write α + β = α − (−β). A negative angle reflects the point in the x-axis: cos(−β) = cos β and sin(−β) = −sin β. That's where the minus sign comes from.
sum-cos.use: It's the base formula: sine, tangent, double angle and half angle all come from it.

sum-sin.title: Sine of a sum and a difference
steps: Complementary angles (adding up to 90°): in a right triangle, the side opposite one acute angle is adjacent to the other. So the sine of one is the cosine of the other.
Apply that to α + β and regroup the bracket.
Use the cosine-of-a-difference formula with 90° − α in place of α.
cos(90° − α) = sin α and sin(90° − α) = cos α (complementary again).
For the difference replace β with −β: cos(−β) = cos β and sin(−β) = −sin β.
sum-sin.use: Find exact sines of non-key angles (15°, 75°, 105°…) and add waves in physics.

sum-tan.title: Tangent of a sum and a difference
steps: Tangent is sine over cosine.
Substitute the sine and cosine formulas.
Divide top and bottom by cos α cos β. The value doesn't change: it's like multiplying by 1.
Simplify each fraction: sin α/cos α = tan α, sin β/cos β = tan β, and anything equal on top and bottom gives 1.
sum-tan.use: Find the angle between two lines from their slopes.

dbl.title: Double angle
steps: Start from the sum formula.
Set β = α (add an angle to itself).
Both terms are equal.
Same trick with the cosine formula.
And with the tangent formula.
dbl.use: Simplify expressions and compute integrals like ∫ sin x cos x dx.

dbl2.title: Double-angle cosine variants
steps: Cosine of the double angle.
Solved from sin²α + cos²α = 1.
Substitute sin²α and collect the cos²α terms.
Now solve for the cosine.
Substitute and collect the sin²α terms.
dbl2.use: Pick the version with only sine or only cosine, depending on what you're given.

half.title: Half angle
steps: A variant of the double-angle cosine, valid for any angle x.
Let x be half of α. Then 2x = α.
Move terms from one side to the other.
Divide by 2 and take the square root. The root has two signs: pick the one for the quadrant where α/2 lies.
Same, starting from cos 2x = 2cos²x − 1.
half.use: Find exact values like sin 15° or cos 22.5° from 30° or 45°.

s2p.title: Sum-to-product
steps: Sum formula.
Difference formula.
Add them: the cos x sin y terms cancel.
Rename. Adding and subtracting the two equations gives x and y.
Substitute. Doing the same with the cosine formulas gives cos α + cos β.
s2p.use: A product is 0 if any factor is 0, which makes equations easier to solve. It also explains the "beats" when two sounds are added.
